#How it works

#The knock

  1. A request arrives. serviceman reads the Host header and the path, and finds the service — the exact hostname first, then wildcards, the longest path prefix wins.
  2. A running service gets the request at once.
  3. A sleeping service is started. Two requests that arrive together start it once.
  4. serviceman waits until the service answers a request — not until its port opens. docker publishes the port before the app inside binds it, so a socket that connects proves only that docker is there.
  5. Up to 2.5 seconds, the caller waits and then gets the answer of the service. It never learns that anything was asleep.
  6. After 2.5 seconds a browser gets the waiting page. Everything else keeps waiting until start_timeout.

#The pages serviceman serves itself

The waiting page and the error page are light or dark, from the same choice the control page keeps, with the same switch in the corner.

An error page of a service that failed is not a dead end: it asks the address again by itself, first after two seconds and then more slowly, up to fifteen. Ask now asks at once. The moment the service answers, the page opens. A page of an address nobody serves does not ask again — nothing will change. Callers that are not browsers get the plain page, never the script.

#The waiting page

The waiting page names the service, counts the seconds, and asks /__serviceman__/status.json every second. The moment the phase turns to running, the page reloads itself and the service answers. A start that fails writes the docker error on the same page.

/__serviceman__/ is the one path serviceman keeps for itself on every service address — for a service mounted at /pdf it lives at /pdf/__serviceman__/.

#The log

Every line has one shape — [time][group_uid][sender] details — and work that causes other work says whose child it is. A whole visit, from the knock to the answer:

[2026-08-21T16:57:07.113Z][cqhldlq3xclh][request_begin] GET /hello {"from":"","host":"whoami.test","ip":"203.0.113.9"}
[2026-08-21T16:57:07.115Z][c8pox602ru6x][group_spawn] parent=cqhldlq3xclh
[2026-08-21T16:57:08.201Z][c8pox602ru6x][docker_run] service=whoami image=demo/whoami remote=vps1
[2026-08-21T16:57:08.255Z][c8pox602ru6x][service_start_end_ok] service=whoami instance=1 remote=vps1 upstream=127.0.0.1:39231 inside=8080 answered=200 took=0.140s
[2026-08-21T16:57:08.269Z][cqhldlq3xclh][request_end] 200 0.156s whoami#1

One grep of the trace shows the whole story; one grep of a sender shows every time it ever happened — and finds the one line of code that writes it. The log lists every sender there is. The file is data/logs/<yyyymmdd>.log next to the config; SERVICEMAN_LOG_DIR moves the folder and SERVICEMAN_LOG_DIR=none turns the file off.

What a service has counted — requests served, how long its last start took, when each copy came up — is kept in data/counters.json, written every few seconds when it moved and once more on the way out. A restart and an edit of the service carry on from those numbers, and a container found still running keeps its age. SERVICEMAN_STATE_DIR moves data/.

Shell on the control page opens a terminal inside the running container: serviceman asks the docker socket on that machine, through the agent's link, for an exec with a TTY and joins it to the pane. The shell lives as long as the pane; closing the pane ends it.

Every decision carries its reason: why a service started, why it was stopped, why another instance was warmed. A container that accepts connections and drops them is named too — [upstream_error] service=deaf hint="nothing inside answers on port 5000, check publish.port" — the sign of a wrong publish.port in the config. A port that answers nothing at all is caught earlier, at the start: nothing answered on 127.0.0.1:41719 — read ECONNRESET — is publish.port (5000) the port it listens on inside?

#The sleep

Every request stamps the service. A stamp is also written when a request finishes, so a long download counts as activity. Every 5 seconds serviceman looks for services that are running, have nothing in flight, and were quiet for longer than stop_after_idle. Those are stopped. always services are never in that list.

#Restarts

A stopped docker service keeps its container, so the next start is docker start. Sockets that pointed to the old container are dropped when the service stops, because docker can give the same host port to somebody else.

When serviceman itself starts, it asks every agent that is dialled in what is already running and adopts it. Nothing is stopped and nothing is started twice. When serviceman is stopped, the containers it started keep running — they are stopped again by the next serviceman, or by hand — and the programs are stopped, because a program nobody watches is an orphan.

#Websockets

A websocket handshake wakes a sleeping service in the same way, then serviceman glues the two sockets together. The connection counts as in-flight for the whole time it is open, so a service with an open socket is never called idle.

#What serviceman never does

serviceman does not delete. It stops containers, it does not remove them, and it never touches volumes, networks or files. The one exception is written in the log: when the image of a docker service changes in the config, the old container is recreated from the new image.

#Failures

A failed start leaves the service in failed with the docker error kept. The next request tries again. If a running service stops answering, serviceman reports 502, forgets the address and starts the service again at the next request.
